reason: Decision guide quotes state Fargate is ideal for long-running applications, microservices or batch processing, and Lambda is optimized for short-lived event-driven tasks with a 15-minute maximum per invocation.
Under Runtime/use cases the guide says Fargate containers can run indefinitely with no hard execution limit, and Lambda has a 15-minute maximum per invocation.
Quote states Lambda is fault-tolerant, invokes the function in a different Availability Zone during a service disruption, and retries when the function throws an error.
The quota row gives 1,024 but the same row says Lambda Managed Instances use a higher limit of 4,096; the claim states 1,024 for every execution environment and drops that exception.
Quotes give up to five filters per event source mapping by default, logically ORed, unmatched records discarded, and a quota increase to up to 10 per event source.
Both sentences are quoted verbatim from the event filtering page: filtering works only with certain event source mappings, and not for Amazon DocumentDB.
Under 'Handling records that don't meet filter criteria' the SQS bullet says Lambda automatically removes unmatched messages and you need not delete them manually.
Pricing page under Lambda Functions Pricing states the free tier includes one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month.
Quote defines the handler as the method that processes events and says a function can contain more than one method but only one handler.
Quote says without lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction in the resource-based policy users get 403 Forbidden, even with the NONE auth type.
Context says you must specify one of the AuthType options; the quotes describe AWS_IAM (identity and resource-based policy) and NONE (no authentication, policy must grant public access).
The 'Best for' row of the comparison table matches both halves of the claim under the correct column headers.
Under Scaling the page says function URLs scale up to the configured concurrency limit, then return HTTP 429 with no built-in queuing, while API Gateway adds queuing and throttling controls.
The quotes support public or IAM auth for function URLs and that API Gateway offers Lambda authorizers, Cognito user pools and OAuth2.0; they do not say these options need (require) API Gateway.
Quote and context state built-in CORS support, no request transformation or validation, and the client receives the response exactly as Lambda returns it.
Under Cost the page says function URLs follow standard Lambda pricing (invocations and compute time) with no additional charge for the URL endpoint.
Quote states that with auth type NONE and a resource-based policy granting public access, any unauthenticated user with the URL can invoke the function.
Quote recommends function URLs for simple applications or prototyping with basic auth and request/response handling and minimal cost and complexity.
Quota row: GetFunction API requests, 100 requests per second, cannot be increased.
Quota row: GetPolicy API requests, 15 requests per second, cannot be increased.
Quote says each Hyperplane ENI supports up to 65,000 connections/ports and Lambda scales ENIs automatically above that.
Quote says Lambda creates a Hyperplane ENI on first attach with a subnet and security group combination and other functions with the same combination can use it.
Quotes give the idempotency definition and the DynamoDB table of recently processed identifiers as the guide's implementation; context gives the duplicate-event reason.
The Note states the 10-second timeout does not apply to provisioned concurrency, SnapStart or Managed Instances, up to 15 minutes, with the 130 seconds or function timeout rule, as claimed.

The quote gives the 10-second Init limit and retry, but the Note right below in context says it does not apply to provisioned concurrency, SnapStart or Managed Instances; the claim drops that condition.
Billing Considerations quotes: no additional cost to access Lambda through an interface endpoint; standard PrivateLink pricing per hour per AZ and per data processed.
Quotes state PrivateLink access to Lambda APIs without IGW, NAT, VPN or Direct Connect, no public IPs, traffic stays on the AWS network, and Invoke can be called from the VPC.
The quote itself adds 'up to 90 minutes for Lambda Managed Instances functions invoked asynchronously or through event source mappings'; the claim states 15 minutes without that exception.
Quote says the timeout limits the entire Invoke phase and the function and all extensions must complete within it.
Quote says with default settings a bad record can block the affected shard for up to one week, and when error handling fails Lambda discards records and continues.
Kinesis parameter table row: BatchSize default 100, Maximum 10,000.
Kinesis page says the event source can buffer up to 5 minutes with a batching window and Lambda invokes on full batch, window expiry, or the 6 MB payload limit.
Kinesis parameter table row: BisectBatchOnFunctionError default false.
DestinationConfig row says Amazon SQS queue or Amazon SNS topic destination for discarded records; the claim does not say these are the only targets.
The quote says more shards lower 'the impact of errors on concurrency'; the claim widens this to 'less impact from errors' and drops the 'on concurrency' scope.
Parameter table row: MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds default -1 (infinite, retention still applies), minimum -1, maximum 604,800.
Parameter table row: MaximumRetryAttempts default -1 (retried until the record expires), minimum -1, maximum 10,000.
Quote says to add a destination to retain failed invocation records and that any SNS topic, SQS queue, S3 bucket or Kafka can be configured.
Quote gives parallelization factor 1 (default) to 10 per shard and the example of factor 2 giving up to 200 concurrent invocations for 100 shards.
Standard iterator bullet: Lambda polls each shard at a base rate of once per second and shares read throughput with other consumers.
